You use the pronouns lui / leur (to him / to her, to them) with verbs like parler à, offrir à, demander à, and give advice.
“Je lui parle” = I talk to him / her
“Je leur écris” = I write to them
je dis, vous dites; participle: dit
“Ça lui plaît” = he / she likes it
To use indirect object pronouns: me, te, lui, nous, vous, leur.
To know which verbs take “à quelqu’un”: parler, téléphoner, offrir, demander…
To put pronouns in the imperative: offre-lui, téléphone-moi.
To tell “le / la” (him / her as direct object) apart from “lui” (to him / to her).
To ask for and give advice about a present.
It’s 12 February. Ioana doesn’t know what to give Julien for Valentine’s Day. At lunchtime she asks Karim and Nathalie for advice.
I have a problem. Friday is Valentine’s Day and I don’t know what to give Julien.
A tie? Karim, that’s not romantic! And Julien never wears a tie.
OK, OK… What does he like? Have you asked him?
No! If I ask him, it’s not a surprise any more.
He loves music, doesn’t he? Buy him concert tickets.
I thought of that. But he already goes to lots of concerts with his pupils.
What about his parents? Phone them. They’ve known him for thirty-one years, they’ll give you an idea!
Good idea! … (She phones.) Hello, Brigitte? It’s Ioana… Yes, I’m calling about Julien…
(After the call) Brigitte gave me a brilliant idea! When he was little, Julien had an old piano. He loved it, but his parents sold it.
You’re not going to give him a piano, surely!
No! But Brigitte sent me a photo of the piano. I’m going to make him a drawing, an architect’s drawing, with his piano and his childhood home.
Now that’s original! He’ll love it, I’m sure.
And tell him you drew it yourself. Men love that.
True. My wife gave me a tie. I’ve never worn it!
of it (“j’y ai pensé” = I thought of that)
go (“tu vas offrir” = you’re going to give)
all the same (“tu ne vas pas… quand même” = surely you’re not going to…)
to please (“ça va lui plaire” = he’ll like it)
of it (“j’en suis sûr” = I’m sure)
Lui = “lwee”, one syllable, the French U quickly followed by “ee”. Not “lu-ee”.
Leur (pronoun) = “lur”. Careful: the pronoun “leur” never takes an -s (“je leur parle”), but the possessive “leurs” does (“leurs enfants”).
In the imperative the pronoun comes after the verb, joined with a hyphen and stressed: “Offre-LUI”, “Téléphone-MOI”, “Dis-LEUR”. The stress falls on the pronoun.
“Ça lui plaît” = “sa lwee PLEH”. As in “s’il vous plaît”, which you already know: it’s the same verb, plaire!
Envoyer: j’envoie = “zhã-VWA”, nous envoyons = “noo-zã-vwa-YÕ”. The y becomes i before a silent e.
Some verbs take “à + person”: parler À quelqu’un (talk TO someone), téléphoner À quelqu’un. When you replace the person, you use an indirect object pronoun, like English “to me, to him, to them”:
I give him / her a present.
“Lui” is for men and women: “Je lui parle” = “I talk to him OR to her”. Context tells you who.
Me, te, nous, vous are the same as in chapter 15. Only the third person has new forms: lui and leur.
2. Le / la or lui? How to choose
It all depends on the verb: does it take a direct object (no “à”) or “à”?
parler à quelqu’un → je lui parle
offrir, donner, envoyer, écrire, prêter (qqch à qqn)

Traps for English speakers: “téléphoner à quelqu’un” (to phone someone) → “je LUI téléphone” (not “je le téléphone”). “Demander à quelqu’un” (to ask someone) → “je LUI demande”. “Répondre à quelqu’un” (to answer someone) → “je LUI réponds”. But “attendre quelqu’un” (to wait FOR someone) → “je L’attends”.
Verbs of giving (donner, offrir, envoyer, écrire, dire…) often have a thing (direct) AND a person (with à): “J’offre un dessin à Julien” → “Je lui offre un dessin”.
3. Where the pronoun goes: the same rules
Lui and leur go exactly where le, la, les went:
I talk to him. (before the verb)
I don’t talk to him. (ne + pronoun + verb + pas)
I phoned him. (before the auxiliary; no agreement!)
I’m going to give him a drawing. (before the infinitive)
In the passé composé the participle does NOT agree with lui / leur (only with a direct object): “Je lui ai écrit” (not “écrite”, even if it’s a woman).
In the AFFIRMATIVE imperative, the pronoun moves AFTER the verb, joined with a hyphen. Me and te become moi and toi:
Ne lui offre pas de fleurs !
Give her flowers! / Don’t give her flowers!
Ne leur dis pas la vérité !
Tell them the truth! / Don’t tell them the truth!
In the affirmative it’s like English: “Call me!” (pronoun after the verb). In the negative, French moves it back in front: “Ne me téléphone pas !”.
5. The verb PLAIRE and giving advice
“Plaire à” (to please) works the opposite way to English “like”: the thing liked is the subject, the person is the indirect object.
Pourquoi tu ne lui offres pas… ? (Why don’t you give him / her…?)
I’m going to send him a card.
Pourquoi Ioana ne demande pas à Julien ?
Un dessin du piano et de la maison d’enfance
Brigitte sent me a photo of the piano.
My wife gave me a tie. I’ve never worn it.
For three evenings Ioana worked in secret on her drawing. She closed her bedroom door and didn’t answer the phone.
Julien sent her messages: “What are you doing? You’re not answering me!” She only wrote back: “I’m working. Surprise!”
In Brigitte’s photo you could see an old black piano in a living room. In front of the piano a little boy of seven was smiling.
Ioana drew the whole house in Annecy: the living room, the window onto the garden, the piano with its sheet music, and little Julien.
Madame Bernard lent her an old gilt frame. “It was Henri’s,” she told her. “He loved beautiful drawings.”
Sophie gave her an idea too: “Write him a little note on the back. Men don’t say so, but they love that.”
On 14 February Julien arrived at Ioana’s with an enormous bunch of roses. He was nervous. He gave her the flowers and a little box of chocolates.
Then Ioana gave him her present, in blue paper. Julien opened it slowly.
He didn’t say anything. He looked at the drawing for a long, long time. His eyes were shining.
“My piano… How did you do it? Did you talk to my mother?”
“I phoned her. She sent me a photo. Look on the back.”
On the back of the drawing Ioana had written in French and Romanian: “For Julien, who taught me to love Lyon. Pentru Julien.”
Julien took her in his arms. “It’s the most beautiful present of my life.”
The next day he hung the drawing above his bed. And he phoned his mother to thank her.
Brigitte laughed on the phone: “I know, darling. Ioana sent me a photo of the drawing yesterday. I’ve shown it to the whole neighbourhood!”
Qui a prêté le cadre à Ioana ?
Où Julien a accroché le dessin ?

Reading text: Valentine’s Day in France
In France, on 14 February, many couples celebrate Valentine’s Day.
Usually people give flowers to the person they love, especially red roses.
They also give them chocolate, perfume or a piece of jewellery.
Lots of men book a table at a restaurant. That evening the restaurants are full!
Some write a love letter. They call their partner sweet names: “mon cœur” (my heart), “mon chéri” (darling), “ma puce” (my flea).
Yes, “ma puce” (my little insect) is a very affectionate word in French!
Single people, on the other hand, don’t always like this day. They say it’s a commercial holiday.
In Romania there’s also Dragobete, on 24 February. It’s the Romanian celebration of love, and it’s older.
Ioana explained Dragobete to Julien. He told her: “Then we have two celebrations. I’m going to give you two presents!”
go (“je vais offrir” = I’m going to give)
I’m going to give you two presents!
